summary: Adversaries may overwrite firmware in components to persist on systems at a layer below the operating system.

name: Pre-OS Boot - Bootkit
summary: Adversaries may use bootkits to persist on systems at a layer below the operating system.

name: Pre-OS Boot - ROMMONkit
summary: Adversaries may abuse the ROM Monitor (ROMMON) by loading an unauthorized firmware with adversary code to provide persistent access and manipulate device behavior.

name: Pre-OS Boot - TFTP Boot
summary: Adversaries may abuse netbooting to load an unauthorized network device operating system from a Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server.

name: Traffic Signaling
summary: Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control.

name: Traffic Signaling - Port Knocking
summary: Adversaries may use port knocking to hide open ports used for persistence or command and control.

name: Traffic Signaling - Socket Filters
summary: Adversaries may attach filters to a network socket to monitor then activate backdoors used for persistence or command and control.

name: Valid Accounts
summary: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

name: Valid Accounts - Default Accounts
summary: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a default account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

name: Valid Accounts - Domain Accounts
summary: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a domain account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

name: Valid Accounts - Local Accounts
summary: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a local account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

name: Valid Accounts - Cloud Accounts
summary: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a cloud account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

name: Office Application Startup
summary: Adversaries may leverage Microsoft Office-based applications for persistence between startups.

name: Office Application Startup - Office Template Macros
summary: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office templates to obtain persistence on a compromised system.

name: Office Application Startup - Office Test
summary: Adversaries may abuse the Microsoft Office 'Office Test' Registry key to obtain persistence on a compromised system.

name: Office Application Startup - Outlook Forms
summary: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook forms to obtain persistence on a compromised system.

name: Office Application Startup - Outlook Home Page
summary: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook's Home Page feature to obtain persistence on a compromised system.

name: Office Application Startup - Outlook Rules
summary: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook rules to obtain persistence on a compromised system.

name: Office Application Startup - Add-ins
summary: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office add-ins to obtain persistence on a compromised system.

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
summary: Adversaries may circumvent mechanisms designed to control privilege elevation to gain higher-level permissions.

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism - Setuid and Setgid
summary: Adversaries may abuse setuid or setgid bits on applications to run code in a more privileged user's context.

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism - Bypass User Account Control
summary: Adversaries may bypass Windows User Account Control (UAC) to elevate process privileges to administrator level.

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism - Sudo and Sudo Caching
summary: Adversaries may abuse sudo caching or the sudoers file to execute commands with elevated privileges.

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism - Elevated Execution with Prompt
summary: Adversaries may leverage the AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API to prompt users for credentials and escalate privileges.

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism - Temporary Elevated Cloud Access
summary: Adversaries may abuse permission configurations to gain temporarily elevated access to cloud resources.

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism - TCC Manipulation
summary: Adversaries may manipulate the Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC) service or database to grant malicious executables elevated permissions.

name: Access Token Manipulation
summary: Adversaries may modify access tokens to operate under a different user or system security context to perform actions and bypass access controls.

name: Access Token Manipulation - Token Impersonation/Theft
summary: Adversaries may duplicate then impersonate another user's existing token to escalate privileges and bypass access controls.

name: Access Token Manipulation - Create Process with Token
summary: Adversaries may create a new process with an existing token to escalate privileges and bypass access controls.

name: Access Token Manipulation - Make and Impersonate Token
summary: Adversaries may create new tokens and impersonate users to escalate privileges and bypass access controls.

name: Access Token Manipulation - Parent PID Spoofing
summary: Adversaries may spoof the parent process identifier (PPID) of a new process to evade defenses or elevate privileges.

name: Access Token Manipulation - SID-History Injection
summary: Adversaries may use SID-History Injection to escalate privileges and bypass access controls.

name: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification
summary: Adversaries may modify the configuration settings of a domain or identity tenant to evade defenses and/or escalate privileges.

name: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification - Group Policy Modification
summary: Adversaries may modify Group Policy Objects (GPOs) to subvert access controls and escalate privileges on a domain.

name: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification - Trust Modification
summary: Adversaries may add or modify domain trusts to escalate privileges and evade defenses.

name: Escape to Host
summary: Adversaries may break out of a container or virtualized environment to gain access to the underlying host.

name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
summary: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities to escalate privileges, including kernel exploits, BYOVD attacks, and container escapes.

name: Hijack Execution Flow
summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the way operating systems run programs.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - DLL Search Order Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the search order used to load DLLs.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - DLL Side-Loading
summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by side-loading DLLs.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - Dylib Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may execute their own payloads by placing a malicious dynamic library (dylib) in a path where a legitimate process expects to find a dylib.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - Executable Installer File Permissions Weakness
summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the binaries used by an installer.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - Dynamic Linker Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking environment variables the dynamic linker uses to load shared libraries.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable
summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking environment variables used to load libraries.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - Path Interception by Search Order Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the search order used to load programs.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - Path Interception by Unquoted Path
summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking vulnerable file path references.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - Services File Permissions Weakness
summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the binaries used by services.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - Services Registry Permissions Weakness
summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the Registry entries used by services.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - COR_PROFILER
summary: Adversaries may leverage the COR_PROFILER environment variable to hijack the execution flow of programs that load the .NET CLR.

name: Hijack Execution Flow - KernelCallbackTable
summary: Adversaries may abuse the KernelCallbackTable to hijack process execution flow and execute malicious code.

name: Process Injection
summary: Adversaries may inject code into processes to evade process-based defenses and possibly elevate privileges.

name: Process Injection - Dynamic-link Library Injection
summary: Adversaries may inject dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) into processes to execute malicious code in the context of another process.

name: Process Injection - Portable Executable Injection
summary: Adversaries may inject portable executables (PEs) into processes to execute malicious code in the context of another process.

name: Process Injection - Thread Execution Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses.

name: Process Injection - Asynchronous Procedure Call
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the asynchronous procedure call (APC) queue to execute code in the context of another process.

name: Process Injection - Thread Local Storage
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via thread local storage (TLS) callbacks to execute code in the context of another process.

name: Process Injection - Ptrace System Calls
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via ptrace system calls to execute code in the context of another process.

name: Process Injection - Proc Memory
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the /proc filesystem to execute code in the context of another process.

name: Process Injection - Extra Window Memory Injection
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via Extra Window Memory (EWM) to evade process-based defenses.

name: Process Injection - Process Hollowing
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into suspended and hollowed processes to evade process-based defenses.

name: Process Injection - Process Doppelgänging
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via process doppelgänging to evade process-based defenses.

name: Process Injection - VDSO Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via VDSO hijacking to execute code in the context of another process.

name: Process Injection - ListPlanting
summary: Adversaries may abuse list-view controls to inject malicious code into processes to evade process-based defenses.

name: Build Image on Host
summary: Adversaries may build a container image directly on a host to bypass defenses that monitor for the retrieval of malicious images from a public registry.

name: Debugger Evasion
summary: Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid debuggers.

name: Delay Execution
summary: Adversaries may employ various time-based methods to evade detection and analysis.

name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
summary: Adversaries may use obfuscated files or information to hide artifacts of an intrusion from analysis and may require separate mechanisms to decode or deobfuscate that information.

name: Direct Volume Access
summary: Adversaries may directly access a volume to bypass file access controls and file system monitoring.

name: Execution Guardrails
summary: Adversaries may use execution guardrails to constrain execution or actions based on adversary supplied and environment specific conditions that are expected to be present on the target.

name: Execution Guardrails - Environmental Keying
summary: Adversaries may environmentally key payloads or other features of malware to evade defenses and constrain execution to a specific target environment.

name: Execution Guardrails - Mutual Exclusion
summary: Adversaries may constrain execution or actions based on the presence of a mutex associated with malware.

name: Exploitation for Stealth
summary: Adversaries may exploit vulnerabilities to evade detection by hiding activity, suppressing logging, or operating within trusted or unmonitored components.

name: Hide Artifacts
summary: Adversaries may attempt to hide artifacts associated with their behaviors to evade detection.

name: Hide Artifacts - Hidden Files and Directories
summary: Adversaries may set files and directories to be hidden to evade detection mechanisms.

name: Hide Artifacts - Hidden Users
summary: Adversaries may use hidden users to hide the presence of user accounts they create or modify.

name: Hide Artifacts - Hidden Window
summary: Adversaries may use hidden windows to conceal malicious activity from the plain sight of users.

name: Hide Artifacts - NTFS File Attributes
summary: Adversaries may use NTFS file attributes to hide their malicious data in order to evade detection.

name: Hide Artifacts - Hidden File System
summary: Adversaries may use a hidden file system to conceal malicious activity from users and security tools.

name: Hide Artifacts - Run Virtual Instance
summary: Adversaries may carry out malicious operations using a virtual instance to avoid detection.

name: Hide Artifacts - VBA Stomping
summary: Adversaries may hide malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) payloads embedded within MS Office documents by replacing the VBA source code with benign data.

name: Hide Artifacts - Email Hiding Rules
summary: Adversaries may use email rules to hide inbound emails in a compromised user's mailbox.

name: Hide Artifacts - Resource Forking
summary: Adversaries may abuse resource forks to hide malicious code or executables to evade detection and bypass security applications.

name: Hide Artifacts - Process Argument Spoofing
summary: Adversaries may attempt to hide process command-line arguments by overwriting process memory.

name: Hide Artifacts - Ignore Process Interrupts
summary: Adversaries may evade defensive mechanisms by executing commands that hide from process interrupt signals.

name: Hide Artifacts - File/Path Exclusions
summary: Adversaries may attempt to hide their file-based artifacts by writing them to specific folders or file names excluded from antivirus (AV) scanning and other defensive capabilities.

name: Hide Artifacts - Bind Mounts
summary: Adversaries may abuse bind mounts on file structures to hide their activity and artifacts from native utilities.

name: Hide Artifacts - Extended Attributes
summary: Adversaries may abuse extended attributes (xattrs) on macOS and Linux to hide their malicious data in order to evade detection.

name: Indicator Removal
summary: Adversaries may selectively delete or modify artifacts generated to reduce indications of their presence and blend in with legitimate activity.

name: Indicator Removal - Clear Command History
summary: Adversaries may clear the command history of a compromised account to conceal the actions undertaken during an intrusion.

name: Indicator Removal - File Deletion
summary: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity.

name: Indicator Removal - Network Share Connection Removal
summary: Adversaries may remove share connections that are no longer useful in order to clean up traces of their operation.

name: Indicator Removal - Timestomp
summary: Adversaries may modify file time attributes to hide new files or changes to existing files.

name: Indicator Removal - Clear Network Connection History and Configurations
summary: Adversaries may clear or remove evidence of malicious network connections in order to clean up traces of their operations.

name: Indicator Removal - Clear Mailbox Data
summary: Adversaries may modify mail and mail application data to remove evidence of their activity.

name: Indicator Removal - Clear Persistence
summary: Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity.

name: Indicator Removal - Relocate Malware
summary: Once a payload is delivered, adversaries may reproduce copies of the same malware on the victim system to remove evidence of their presence and/or avoid defenses.

name: Indirect Command Execution
summary: Adversaries may abuse utilities that allow for command execution to bypass security restrictions that limit the use of command-line interpreters.

name: Masquerading
summary: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools.

name: Masquerading - Invalid Code Signature
summary: Adversaries may attempt to mimic features of valid code signatures to increase the chance of deceiving a user, analyst, or tool.

name: Masquerading - Right-to-Left Override
summary: Adversaries may abuse the right-to-left override (RTLO or RLO) character (U+202E) to disguise a string and/or file name to make it appear benign.

name: Masquerading - Rename Legitimate Utilities
summary: Adversaries may rename legitimate / system utilities to try to evade security mechanisms concerning the usage of those utilities.

name: Masquerading - Masquerade Task or Service
summary: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the name of a task or service to make it appear legitimate or benign.

name: Disable or Modify System Firewall
summary: Adversaries may disable or modify host-based or network firewalls to impair defensive mechanisms and enable further action.

name: Disable or Modify System Firewall - Cloud Firewall
summary: Adversaries may disable or modify a firewall within a cloud environment to bypass controls that limit access to cloud resources.

name: Disable or Modify System Firewall - Network Device Firewall
summary: Adversaries may disable network device-based firewall mechanisms entirely or add, delete, or modify particular rules in order to bypass controls limiting network usage.

name: Disable or Modify System Firewall - Windows Host Firewall
summary: Adversaries may disable or modify the Windows host firewall to bypass controls limiting network usage.

name: Disable or Modify Tools
summary: Adversaries may disable, degrade, or tamper with security tools or applications to impair or reduce visibility of defensive capabilities.

name: Disable or Modify Tools - Disable or Modify Windows Event Log
summary: Adversaries may disable or modify the Windows Event Log to limit data that can be leveraged for detections and audits.

name: Disable or Modify Tools - Disable or Modify Cloud Log
summary: An adversary may disable or modify cloud logging capabilities and integrations to limit what data is collected on their activities and avoid detection.

name: Disable or Modify Tools - Modify or Spoof Tool UI
summary: Adversaries may spoof or manipulate security tool user interfaces (UIs) to falsely indicate tools are functioning normally and delay detection and response.

name: Disable or Modify Tools - Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log
summary: Adversaries may disable or modify the Linux Audit system to hide malicious activity and avoid detection.

name: Disable or Modify Tools - Clear Windows Event Logs
summary: Adversaries may clear Windows Event Logs to hide the activity of an intrusion.

name: Disable or Modify Tools - Clear Linux or Mac System Logs
summary: Adversaries may clear system logs to hide evidence of an intrusion.

name: Downgrade Attack
summary: Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls.

name: Exploitation for Defense Impairment
summary: Adversaries may exploit vulnerabilities in security software, infrastructure, or defensive components to degrade, disable, or otherwise impair their ability to prevent, detect, or respond to malicious activity.

name: File and Directory Permissions Modification
summary: Adversaries may modify file or directory permissions/attributes to evade access control lists (ACLs) and access protected files.

name: File and Directory Permissions Modification - Windows Permissions
summary: Adversaries may modify file or directory permissions/attributes to evade access control lists (ACLs) and access protected files on Windows systems.

name: File and Directory Permissions Modification - Linux and Mac Permissions
summary: Adversaries may modify file or directory permissions/attributes to evade access control lists (ACLs) and access protected files on Linux and Mac systems.

name: Modify Authentication Process
summary: Adversaries may modify authentication mechanisms and processes to access user credentials or enable otherwise unwarranted access to accounts.

name: Modify Authentication Process - Domain Controller Authentication
summary: Adversaries may patch the authentication process on a domain controller to bypass the typical authentication mechanisms and enable access to accounts.

name: Modify Authentication Process - Password Filter DLL
summary: Adversaries may register malicious password filter dynamic link libraries (DLLs) into the authentication process to acquire user credentials as they are validated.

name: Modify Authentication Process - Pluggable Authentication Modules
summary: Adversaries may modify pluggable authentication modules (PAM) to access user credentials or enable otherwise unwarranted access to accounts.

name: Modify Authentication Process - Network Device Authentication
summary: Adversaries may use Patch System Image to hard code a password in the operating system, thus bypassing native authentication mechanisms for local accounts on network devices.

name: Modify Authentication Process - Reversible Encryption
summary: An adversary may abuse Active Directory authentication encryption properties to gain access to credentials on Windows systems.

name: Modify Authentication Process - Multi-Factor Authentication
summary: Adversaries may disable or modify multi-factor authentication (MFA) mechanisms to enable persistent access to compromised accounts.

name: Modify Authentication Process - Hybrid Identity
summary: Adversaries may patch, modify, or otherwise backdoor cloud authentication processes that are tied to on-premises user identities in order to bypass typical authentication mechanisms, access credentials, and enable persistent access to accounts.

name: Modify Authentication Process - Network Provider DLL
summary: Adversaries may register malicious network provider dynamic link libraries (DLLs) to capture cleartext user credentials during the authentication process.

name: Modify Authentication Process - Conditional Access Policies
summary: Adversaries may disable or modify conditional access policies to enable persistent access to compromised accounts.

name: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure
summary: An adversary may attempt to modify a cloud account's compute service infrastructure to evade defenses.

name: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure - Create Snapshot
summary: An adversary may create a snapshot or data backup within a cloud account to evade defenses.

name: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure - Create Cloud Instance
summary: An adversary may create a new instance or virtual machine (VM) within the compute service of a cloud account to evade defenses.

name: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure - Delete Cloud Instance
summary: An adversary may delete a cloud instance after they have performed malicious activities in an attempt to evade detection and remove evidence of their presence.

name: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure - Revert Cloud Instance
summary: An adversary may revert changes made to a cloud instance after they have performed malicious activities in attempt to evade detection and remove evidence of their presence.

name: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure - Modify Cloud Compute Configurations
summary: Adversaries may modify settings that directly affect the size, locations, and resources available to cloud compute infrastructure in order to evade defenses.

name: Modify Cloud Resource Hierarchy
summary: Adversaries may attempt to modify hierarchical structures in infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) environments in order to evade defenses.

name: Modify Registry
summary: Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry as part of a variety of other techniques to aid in defense evasion, persistence, and execution.

name: Modify System Image
summary: Adversaries may make changes to the operating system of embedded network devices to weaken defenses and provide new capabilities for themselves.

name: Modify System Image - Patch System Image
summary: Adversaries may modify the operating system of a network device to introduce new capabilities or weaken existing defenses.

name: Modify System Image - Downgrade System Image
summary: Adversaries may install an older version of the operating system of a network device to weaken security.

name: Network Boundary Bridging
summary: Adversaries may bridge network boundaries by compromising perimeter network devices or internal devices responsible for network segmentation.

name: Network Boundary Bridging - Network Address Translation Traversal
summary: Adversaries may bridge network boundaries by modifying a network device’s Network Address Translation (NAT) configuration.

name: Plist File Modification
summary: Adversaries may modify property list files (plist files) to enable other malicious activity, while also potentially evading and bypassing system defenses.

name: Prevent Command History Logging
summary: Adversaries may impair command history logging to hide commands they run on a compromised system.

name: Rogue Domain Controller
summary: Adversaries may register a rogue Domain Controller to enable manipulation of Active Directory data.

name: Safe Mode Boot
summary: Adversaries may abuse Windows safe mode to disable endpoint defenses.

name: Subvert Trust Controls
summary: Adversaries may undermine security controls that will either warn users of untrusted activity or prevent execution of untrusted programs.

name: Subvert Trust Controls - Gatekeeper Bypass
summary: Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs.

name: Subvert Trust Controls - Code Signing
summary: Adversaries may create, acquire, or steal code signing materials to sign their malware or tools.

name: Subvert Trust Controls - SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may tamper with SIP and trust provider components to mislead the operating system and application control tools when conducting signature validation checks.

name: Subvert Trust Controls - Install Root Certificate
summary: Adversaries may install a root certificate on a compromised system to avoid warnings when connecting to adversary controlled web servers.

name: Subvert Trust Controls - Mark-of-the-Web Bypass
summary: Adversaries may abuse specific file formats to subvert Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) controls.

name: Subvert Trust Controls - Code Signing Policy Modification
summary: Adversaries may modify code signing policies to enable execution of unsigned or self-signed code.

name: Weaken Encryption
summary: Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications.

name: Weaken Encryption - Reduce Key Space
summary: Adversaries may reduce the level of effort required to decrypt data transmitted over the network by reducing the cipher strength of encrypted communications.

name: Weaken Encryption - Disable Crypto Hardware
summary: Adversaries disable a network device’s dedicated hardware encryption, which may enable them to leverage weaknesses in software encryption in order to reduce the effort involved in collecting, manipulating, and exfiltrating transmitted data.

name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
summary: Adversaries position themselves between networked devices to intercept and relay communications, enabling credential capture and session hijacking.

name: Adversary-in-the-Middle - Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
summary: Adversaries spoof authoritative name resolution sources to force communication through adversary-controlled systems and collect or relay authentication materials.

name: Adversary-in-the-Middle - ARP Cache Poisoning
summary: Adversaries poison ARP caches to position themselves between networked devices and enable follow-on behaviors like network sniffing or data manipulation.

name: Adversary-in-the-Middle - DHCP Spoofing
summary: Adversaries spoof DHCP traffic to redirect network traffic to adversary-owned systems and collect credentials sent over insecure protocols.

name: Adversary-in-the-Middle - Evil Twin
summary: Adversaries host seemingly genuine Wi-Fi access points to deceive users into connecting to malicious networks and support follow-on behaviors.

name: Brute Force
summary: Adversaries systematically guess passwords to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.

name: Brute Force - Password Guessing
summary: Adversaries with no prior knowledge of legitimate credentials guess passwords to attempt access to accounts.

name: Brute Force - Password Cracking
summary: Adversaries use password cracking to recover usable credentials, such as plaintext passwords, from obtained password hashes.

name: Brute Force - Password Spraying
summary: Adversaries use a single or small list of commonly used passwords against many different accounts to attempt to acquire valid credentials.

name: Brute Force - Credential Stuffing
summary: Adversaries use credentials obtained from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to gain access to target accounts through credential overlap.

name: Credentials from Password Stores
summary: Adversaries search for common password storage locations, such as password managers and cloud secrets vaults, to obtain user credentials.

name: Credentials from Password Stores - Keychain
summary: Adversaries acquire credentials from macOS Keychain, which stores account names, passwords, and other sensitive data.

name: Credentials from Password Stores - Securityd Memory
summary: Adversaries with root access read securityd's memory to gather credentials and decrypt the user's logon keychain.

name: Credentials from Password Stores - Credentials from Web Browsers
summary: Adversaries acquire credentials from web browsers by reading files specific to the target browser.

name: Credentials from Password Stores - Windows Credential Manager
summary: Adversaries acquire credentials from the Windows Credential Manager, which stores credentials for websites, applications, and devices.

name: Credentials from Password Stores - Password Managers
summary: Adversaries acquire user credentials from third-party password managers, which store credentials in encrypted databases.

name: Credentials from Password Stores - Cloud Secrets Management Stores
summary: Adversaries acquire credentials from cloud-native secret management solutions such as AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, and Azure Key Vault.

name: Exploitation for Credential Access
summary: Adversaries exploit software vulnerabilities to collect credentials from systems or services.

name: Forced Authentication
summary: Adversaries gather credential material by invoking or forcing a user to automatically provide authentication information through an interceptable mechanism.

name: Forge Web Credentials
summary: Adversaries forge credential materials, such as session cookies or SAML tokens, to gain access to web applications or Internet services.

name: Forge Web Credentials - Web Cookies
summary: Adversaries forge web cookies to gain access to web applications or Internet services.

name: Forge Web Credentials - SAML Tokens
summary: Adversaries forge SAML tokens with any permissions claims and lifetimes if they possess a valid SAML token-signing certificate.

name: Input Capture
summary: Adversaries use methods of capturing user input, such as keylogging or GUI input capture, to obtain credentials or collect information.

name: Input Capture - Keylogging
summary: Adversaries log user keystrokes to intercept credentials as the user types them.

name: Input Capture - GUI Input Capture
summary: Adversaries mimic common operating system GUI components to prompt users for credentials with a seemingly legitimate prompt.

name: Input Capture - Web Portal Capture
summary: Adversaries install code on externally facing portals, such as VPN login pages, to capture and transmit user credentials.

name: Input Capture - Credential API Hooking
summary: Adversaries hook into API functions to collect user credentials from parameters that reveal authentication information.

name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
summary: Adversaries target multi-factor authentication mechanisms to gain access to credentials that can be used to access systems and network resources.

name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
summary: Adversaries attempt to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) mechanisms and gain access to accounts by generating MFA requests sent to users.

name: Network Sniffing
summary: Adversaries passively sniff network traffic to capture information about an environment, including authentication material passed over the network.

name: OS Credential Dumping
summary: Adversaries dump credentials from OS caches, memory, or structures to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or cleartext password.

name: OS Credential Dumping - LSASS Memory
summary: Adversaries access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS).

name: OS Credential Dumping - Security Account Manager
summary: Adversaries extract credential material from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database via in-memory techniques or the Windows Registry.

name: OS Credential Dumping - NTDS
summary: Adversaries access or copy the Active Directory domain database (NTDS.dit) to steal credential information and other domain data.

name: OS Credential Dumping - LSA Secrets
summary: Adversaries with SYSTEM access access Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, which can contain credentials for service accounts.

name: OS Credential Dumping - Cached Domain Credentials
summary: Adversaries access cached domain credentials used to allow authentication when a domain controller is unavailable.

name: OS Credential Dumping - DCSync
summary: Adversaries abuse a Windows Domain Controller's API to simulate the replication process and access credentials and other sensitive information.

name: OS Credential Dumping - Proc Filesystem
summary: Adversaries gather credentials from the proc filesystem (/proc) on Linux systems by reading process memory maps and mem files.

name: OS Credential Dumping - /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
summary: Adversaries dump the contents of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to enable offline password cracking.

name: Steal Application Access Token
summary: Adversaries can steal application access tokens as a means of acquiring credentials to access remote systems and resources.

name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
summary: Adversaries steal or forge certificates used for authentication to access remote systems or resources.

name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
summary: Adversaries subvert Kerberos authentication by stealing or forging Kerberos tickets to enable Pass the Ticket.

name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets - Golden Ticket
summary: Adversaries with the KRBTGT account password hash forge Kerberos ticket-granting tickets (TGTs) to generate authentication material for any account.

name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets - Silver Ticket
summary: Adversaries with the password hash of a target service account forge Kerberos ticket-granting service (TGS) tickets.

name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets - Kerberoasting
summary: Adversaries abuse a valid Kerberos TGT or sniff network traffic to obtain a TGS ticket that may be vulnerable to brute force.

name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets - AS-REP Roasting
summary: Adversaries reveal credentials of accounts with disabled Kerberos preauthentication by cracking Kerberos messages.

name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets - Ccache Files
summary: Adversaries steal Kerberos tickets stored in credential cache files (ccache) used for short-term storage of a user's active session credentials.

name: Steal Web Session Cookie
summary: Adversaries steal web application or service session cookies to gain access as an authenticated user without needing credentials.

name: Unsecured Credentials
summary: Adversaries search compromised systems to find and obtain insecurely stored credentials in files, registries, or other artifacts.

name: Unsecured Credentials - Credentials In Files
summary: Adversaries search local file systems and remote file shares for files containing insecurely stored credentials.

name: Unsecured Credentials - Credentials in Registry
summary: Adversaries search the Windows Registry for insecurely stored credentials and passwords used by programs or services.

name: Unsecured Credentials - Shell History
summary: Adversaries search the command history on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials.

name: Unsecured Credentials - Private Keys
summary: Adversaries search for private key certificate files on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials.

name: Unsecured Credentials - Cloud Instance Metadata API
summary: Adversaries access the Cloud Instance Metadata API to obtain credentials and other sensitive information from cloud instances.

name: Account Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of valid accounts, usernames, or email addresses on a system or within a compromised environment.

name: Account Discovery - Local Account
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of local system accounts.

name: Account Discovery - Domain Account
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of domain accounts.

name: Account Discovery - Email Account
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of email addresses and accounts.

name: Account Discovery - Cloud Account
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of cloud accounts.

name: Application Window Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of open application windows to identify potential data to collect and security tooling.

name: Browser Information Discovery
summary: Adversaries may enumerate information about browsers to learn more about compromised environments, including bookmarks, accounts, and browsing history.

name: Cloud Infrastructure Discovery
summary: An adversary may attempt to discover infrastructure and resources that are available within an infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) environment.

name: Cloud Service Dashboard
summary: An adversary may use a cloud service dashboard GUI with stolen credentials to gain useful information from an operational cloud environment.

name: Cloud Service Discovery
summary: An adversary may attempt to enumerate the cloud services running on a system after gaining access.

name: Cloud Storage Object Discovery
summary: Adversaries may enumerate objects in cloud storage infrastructure to identify sensitive data for collection.

name: Container and Resource Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to discover containers and other resources available within a containers environment.

name: Device Driver Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to enumerate local device drivers on a victim host to identify security tools or exploitable vulnerabilities.

name: Domain Trust Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to gather information on domain trust relationships to identify lateral movement opportunities.

name: File and Directory Discovery
summary: Adversaries may enumerate files and directories or search in specific locations of a host or network share for certain information within a file system.

name: Process Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get information about running processes on a system to understand common software and shape follow-on behaviors.

name: System Time Discovery
summary: An adversary may gather the system time and/or time zone settings from a local or remote system.

name: Software Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of software and software versions that are installed on a system or in a cloud environment.

name: Software Discovery - Security Software Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of security software, configurations, defensive tools, and sensors that are installed on a system or in a cloud environment.

name: Software Discovery - Backup Software Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of backup software or configurations that are installed on a system.

name: Remote System Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by IP address, hostname, or other logical identifier on a network for lateral movement.

name: Password Policy Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to access detailed information about the password policy used within an enterprise network or cloud environment.

name: Network Service Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices to identify exploitable targets.

name: System Network Connections Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of network connections to or from the compromised system they are currently accessing or from remote systems.

name: System Network Configuration Discovery
summary: Adversaries may look for details about the network configuration and settings of systems they access or use, such as IP addresses and network interfaces.

name: Permission Groups Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to discover group and permission settings to determine which user accounts and groups have elevated permissions.

name: System Owner/User Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to identify the primary user, currently logged in user, set of users that commonly uses a system, or whether a user is actively using the system.

name: System Information Discovery
summary: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, and architecture.

name: Exploitation of Remote Services
summary: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in remote services to gain unauthorized access to internal systems.

name: Internal Spearphishing
summary: Adversaries may use internal spearphishing to gain access to additional information or compromise other users within the same organization.

name: Lateral Tool Transfer
summary: Adversaries may transfer tools or other files between systems in a compromised environment to stage tools or other files.

name: Remote Service Session Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may take control of preexisting sessions with remote services to move laterally in an environment.

name: Remote Service Session Hijacking - SSH Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user's SSH session to move laterally within an environment.

name: Remote Service Session Hijacking - RDP Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user's remote desktop session to move laterally within an environment.

name: Remote Services
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a service that accepts remote connections, such as telnet, SSH, and VNC. The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

name: Remote Services: Distributed Component Object Model
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote machines by taking advantage of Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

name: Remote Services: SSH
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into remote machines using Secure Shell (SSH). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

name: Remote Services: VNC
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC).

name: Remote Services: Windows Remote Management
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

name: Remote Services: Cloud Services
summary: Adversaries may log into accessible cloud services within a compromised environment using Valid Accounts that are synchronized with or federated to on-premises user identities. The adversary may then perform management actions or access cloud-hosted resources as the logged-on user.

name: Remote Services: Direct Cloud VM Connections
summary: Adversaries may leverage Valid Accounts to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods.

name: Taint Shared Content
summary: Adversaries may deliver payloads to remote systems by adding content to shared storage locations, such as network drives or internal code repositories.

name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
summary: Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as password hashes and Kerberos tickets, to move laterally within an environment.

name: Use Alternate Authentication Material - Application Access Token
summary: Adversaries may use stolen application access tokens to bypass the typical authentication process and access restricted accounts, information, or services.

name: Use Alternate Authentication Material - Pass the Hash
summary: Adversaries may pass the hash using stolen password hashes to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls.

name: Use Alternate Authentication Material - Pass the Ticket
summary: Adversaries may pass the ticket using stolen Kerberos tickets to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls.

name: Use Alternate Authentication Material - Web Session Cookie
summary: Adversaries may use stolen web session cookies to bypass the authentication process of a web application and impersonate the user.

name: Software Deployment Tools
summary: Adversaries may gain access to and use centralized software suites installed within an enterprise to execute commands and move laterally through the network.

name: Archive Collected Data
summary: Adversaries compress and/or encrypt collected data prior to exfiltration to obfuscate the data and minimize network transfer size.

name: Archive Collected Data - Archive via Utility
summary: Adversaries use utilities to compress and/or encrypt collected data prior to exfiltration.

name: Archive Collected Data - Archive via Library
summary: Adversaries compress or encrypt collected data using third-party libraries prior to exfiltration.

name: Archive Collected Data - Archive via Custom Method
summary: Adversaries compress or encrypt collected data using custom methods, such as XOR encryption or stream ciphers, prior to exfiltration.

name: Audio Capture
summary: Adversaries leverage peripheral devices or applications to capture audio recordings for gathering sensitive information.

name: Automated Collection
summary: Adversaries use automated techniques, such as scripting, to collect internal data based on predefined criteria like file type, location, or name.

name: Browser Session Hijacking
summary: Adversaries exploit browser vulnerabilities and functionality to change content, modify user behavior, and intercept information.

name: Clipboard Data
summary: Adversaries collect data stored in the clipboard from users copying information within or between applications.

name: Data from Cloud Storage
summary: Adversaries access data from cloud storage services, which can contain a wide variety of files and information.

name: Data from Configuration Repository
summary: Adversaries collect data from configuration repositories, which store parameters that determine device and network operations.

name: Data from Configuration Repository - SNMP (MIB Dump)
summary: Adversaries target the Management Information Base (MIB) to collect and mine valuable information in SNMP-managed networks.

name: Data from Configuration Repository - Network Device Configuration Dump
summary: Adversaries access network configuration files to collect sensitive data about the device and the network.

name: Data from Information Repositories
summary: Adversaries leverage information repositories, such as Confluence, SharePoint, and code repositories, to mine valuable information for further objectives.

name: Data from Information Repositories - Confluence
summary: Adversaries leverage Confluence repositories to mine valuable information, often found in development environments.

name: Data from Information Repositories - Sharepoint
summary: Adversaries leverage SharePoint repositories to mine valuable information about internal network structure and systems.

name: Data from Information Repositories - Code Repositories
summary: Adversaries leverage code repositories, such as GitHub and GitLab, to collect valuable source code and information.

name: Data from Information Repositories - Customer Relationship Management Software
summary: Adversaries leverage Customer Relationship Management (CRM) software to mine valuable customer and business information.

name: Data from Information Repositories - Messaging Applications
summary: Adversaries leverage chat and messaging applications, such as Microsoft Teams and Slack, to mine valuable information.

name: Data from Information Repositories - Databases
summary: Adversaries leverage databases, hosted on-premises or in the cloud, to mine valuable information.

name: Data from Local System
summary: Adversaries search local system sources, such as file systems and configuration files, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to exfiltration.

name: Data from Network Shared Drive
summary: Adversaries search network shares on compromised systems to find files of interest for collection prior to exfiltration.

name: Data from Removable Media
summary: Adversaries search connected removable media on compromised systems to find files of interest for collection prior to exfiltration.

name: Data Staged
summary: Adversaries stage collected data in a central location or directory prior to exfiltration.

name: Data Staged - Local Data Staging
summary: Adversaries stage collected data in a central location or directory on the local system prior to exfiltration.

name: Data Staged - Remote Data Staging
summary: Adversaries stage data collected from multiple systems in a central location or directory on one system prior to exfiltration.

name: Email Collection
summary: Adversaries target user email to collect sensitive information, including trade secrets and personal data.

name: Email Collection - Local Email Collection
summary: Adversaries target user email on local systems to collect sensitive information from files such as Outlook storage or cache files.

name: Email Collection - Remote Email Collection
summary: Adversaries target Exchange servers, Office 365, or Google Workspace to collect sensitive email information.

name: Email Collection - Email Forwarding Rule
summary: Adversaries set up email forwarding rules to collect sensitive information and maintain persistent access to victim emails.

name: Screen Capture
summary: Adversaries take screen captures of the desktop to gather information over the course of an operation.

name: Video Capture
summary: Adversaries leverage peripheral devices or applications to capture video recordings for gathering information.

name: Application Layer Protocol
summary: Adversaries may communicate using OSI application layer protocols to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

name: Application Layer Protocol - Web Protocols
summary: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with web traffic to avoid detection by blending in with existing traffic.

name: Application Layer Protocol - File Transfer Protocols
summary: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with transferring files to avoid detection by blending in with existing traffic.

name: Application Layer Protocol - Mail Protocols
summary: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with electronic mail delivery to avoid detection by blending in with existing traffic.

name: Application Layer Protocol - DNS
summary: Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection by blending in with existing traffic.

name: Application Layer Protocol - Publish/Subscribe Protocols
summary: Adversaries may communicate using publish/subscribe (pub/sub) application layer protocols to avoid detection by blending in with existing traffic.

name: Communication Through Removable Media
summary: Adversaries can perform command and control between compromised hosts on potentially disconnected networks using removable media to transfer commands from system to system.

name: Data Encoding
summary: Adversaries may encode data to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect.

name: Data Encoding - Standard Encoding
summary: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect.

name: Data Encoding - Non-Standard Encoding
summary: Adversaries may encode data with a non-standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect.

name: Data Obfuscation
summary: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.

name: Data Obfuscation - Junk Data
summary: Adversaries may add junk data to protocols used for command and control to make detection more difficult.

name: Data Obfuscation - Steganography
summary: Adversaries may use steganographic techniques to hide command and control traffic to make detection efforts more difficult.

name: Data Obfuscation - Protocol or Service Impersonation
summary: Adversaries may impersonate legitimate protocols or web service traffic to disguise command and control activity and thwart analysis efforts.

name: Dynamic Resolution
summary: Adversaries may dynamically establish connections to command and control infrastructure to evade common detections and remediations.

name: Dynamic Resolution - Fast Flux DNS
summary: Adversaries may use Fast Flux DNS to hide a command and control channel behind an array of rapidly changing IP addresses linked to a single domain resolution.

name: Dynamic Resolution - Domain Generation Algorithms
summary: Adversaries may make use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to dynamically identify a destination domain for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains.

name: Dynamic Resolution - DNS Calculation
summary: Adversaries may perform calculations on addresses returned in DNS results to determine which port and IP address to use for command and control, rather than relying on a predetermined port number or the actual returned IP address.

name: Encrypted Channel
summary: Adversaries may employ an encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

name: Encrypted Channel - Symmetric Cryptography
summary: Adversaries may employ a known symmetric encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

name: Encrypted Channel - Asymmetric Cryptography
summary: Adversaries may employ a known asymmetric encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

name: Fallback Channels
summary: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.

name: Hide Infrastructure
summary: Adversaries may manipulate network traffic in order to hide and evade detection of their C2 infrastructure.

name: Ingress Tool Transfer
summary: Adversaries may transfer tools or other files from an external system into a compromised environment.

name: Multi-Stage Channels
summary: Adversaries may create multiple stages for command and control that are employed under different conditions or for certain functions.

name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
summary: Adversaries may use an OSI non-application layer protocol for communication between host and C2 server or among infected hosts within a network.

name: Non-Standard Port
summary: Adversaries may communicate using a protocol and port pairing that are typically not associated.

name: Protocol Tunneling
summary: Adversaries may tunnel network communications to and from a victim system within a separate protocol to avoid detection/network filtering and/or enable access to otherwise unreachable systems.

name: Proxy
summary: Adversaries may use a connection proxy to direct network traffic between systems or act as an intermediary for network communications to a command and control server to avoid direct connections to their infrastructure.

name: Proxy - Internal Proxy
summary: Adversaries may use an internal proxy to direct command and control traffic between two or more systems in a compromised environment.

name: Proxy - External Proxy
summary: Adversaries may use an external proxy to act as an intermediary for network communications to a command and control server to avoid direct connections to their infrastructure.

name: Proxy - Multi-hop Proxy
summary: Adversaries may chain together multiple proxies to disguise the source of malicious traffic.

name: Proxy - Domain Fronting
summary: Adversaries may take advantage of routing schemes in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) and other services which host multiple domains to obfuscate the intended destination of HTTPS traffic or traffic tunneled through HTTPS.

name: Remote Access Tools
summary: An adversary may use legitimate remote access tools to establish an interactive command and control channel within a network.

name: Remote Access Tools - IDE Tunneling
summary: Adversaries may abuse Integrated Development Environment (IDE) software with remote development features to establish an interactive command and control channel on target systems within a network.

name: Remote Access Tools - Remote Desktop Software
summary: An adversary may use legitimate desktop support software to establish an interactive command and control channel to target systems within networks.

name: Remote Access Tools - Remote Access Hardware
summary: An adversary may use legitimate remote access hardware to establish an interactive command and control channel to target systems within networks.

name: Web Service
summary: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for relaying data to/from a compromised system.

name: Web Service - Dead Drop Resolver
summary: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service to host information that points to additional command and control (C2) infrastructure.

name: Web Service - Bidirectional Communication
summary: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel.

name: Web Service - One-Way Communication
summary: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to a compromised system without receiving return output over the Web service channel.

name: Automated Exfiltration
summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data through automated processing after being gathered during collection.

name: Automated Exfiltration - Traffic Duplication
summary: Adversaries may leverage traffic mirroring to automate data exfiltration over compromised infrastructure.

name: Data Transfer Size Limits
summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data in fixed-size chunks or limit packet sizes to avoid triggering network data transfer threshold alerts.

name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a different protocol than that of the existing command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol - Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a symmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol - Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an asymmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol - Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an un-encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an existing command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a different network medium than the command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium - Exfiltration Over Bluetooth
summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over Bluetooth rather than the command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data via a physical medium, such as a removable drive.

name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium - Exfiltration over USB
summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a USB connected physical device.

name: Exfiltration Over Web Service
summary: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service to exfiltrate data rather than their primary command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Web Service - Exfiltration to Code Repository
summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a code repository rather than over their primary command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Web Service - Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a cloud storage service rather than over their primary command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Web Service - Exfiltration to Text Storage Sites
summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to text storage sites instead of their primary command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Web Service - Exfiltration Over Webhook
summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a webhook endpoint rather than over their primary command and control channel.

name: Scheduled Transfer
summary: Adversaries may schedule data exfiltration to be performed only at certain times of day or at certain intervals to blend with normal activity.

name: Transfer Data to Cloud Account
summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data by transferring it to another cloud account they control on the same service.

name: Data Destruction
summary: Adversaries destroy data and files on specific systems or across a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources.

name: Data Destruction - Lifecycle-Triggered Deletion
summary: Adversaries modify the lifecycle policies of a cloud storage bucket to destroy all objects stored within.

name: Data Encrypted for Impact
summary: Adversaries encrypt data on target systems or across a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources, typically for ransomware.

name: Service Stop
summary: Adversaries stop or disable services on a system to render those services unavailable to legitimate users.

name: Inhibit System Recovery
summary: Adversaries delete or remove built-in data and turn off services designed to aid in the recovery of a corrupted system to prevent recovery.

name: Defacement
summary: Adversaries modify visual content available internally or externally to an enterprise network, affecting the integrity of the original content.

name: Defacement - Internal Defacement
summary: Adversaries deface systems internal to an organization to intimidate or mislead users, discrediting the integrity of the systems.

name: Defacement - External Defacement
summary: Adversaries deface systems external to an organization to deliver messaging, intimidate, or otherwise mislead users, causing distrust in the system's integrity.

name: Firmware Corruption
summary: Adversaries overwrite or corrupt the flash memory contents of system BIOS or other firmware in devices to render them inoperable or unable to boot.

name: Resource Hijacking
summary: Adversaries leverage the resources of co-opted systems to complete resource-intensive tasks, impacting system and hosted service availability.

name: Network Denial of Service
summary: Adversaries perform Network Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of targeted resources to users.

name: Network Denial of Service - Direct Network Flood
summary: Adversaries attempt to cause a denial of service (DoS) by directly sending a high-volume of network traffic to a target.

name: Network Denial of Service - Reflection Amplification
summary: Adversaries attempt to cause a denial of service (DoS) by reflecting a high-volume of network traffic to a target using a third-party server intermediary.

name: Endpoint Denial of Service
summary: Adversaries perform Endpoint Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of services to users.

name: Endpoint Denial of Service - OS Exhaustion Flood
summary: Adversaries launch a denial of service (DoS) attack targeting an endpoint's operating system to exhaust its finite resources.

name: Endpoint Denial of Service - Service Exhaustion Flood
summary: Adversaries target network services provided by systems to conduct a denial of service (DoS) by exhausting service resources.

name: Endpoint Denial of Service - Application Exhaustion Flood
summary: Adversaries target resource-intensive features of applications to cause a denial of service (DoS), denying availability to those applications.

name: Endpoint Denial of Service - Application or System Exploitation
summary: Adversaries exploit software vulnerabilities that can cause an application or system to crash and deny availability to users.

name: System Shutdown/Reboot
summary: Adversaries shutdown or reboot systems to interrupt access to, or aid in the destruction of, those systems.

name: Account Access Removal
summary: Adversaries interrupt availability of system and network resources by inhibiting access to accounts utilized by legitimate users.

name: Disk Wipe
summary: Adversaries wipe or corrupt raw disk data on specific systems or across a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

name: Disk Wipe - Disk Content Wipe
summary: Adversaries erase the contents of storage devices on specific systems or across a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

name: Disk Wipe - Disk Structure Wipe
summary: Adversaries corrupt or wipe the disk data structures on a hard drive necessary to boot a system, interrupting availability to system and network resources.

name: Data Manipulation
summary: Adversaries insert, delete, or manipulate data to influence external outcomes or hide activity, threatening the integrity of the data.

name: Data Manipulation - Stored Data Manipulation
summary: Adversaries insert, delete, or manipulate data at rest to influence external outcomes or hide activity, threatening data integrity.

name: Data Manipulation - Transmitted Data Manipulation
summary: Adversaries alter data en route to storage or other systems to manipulate external outcomes or hide activity, threatening data integrity.

name: Data Manipulation - Runtime Data Manipulation
summary: Adversaries modify systems to manipulate data as it is accessed and displayed to an end user, threatening data integrity.

name: Financial Theft
summary: Adversaries steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods for financial gain.

name: Email Bombing
summary: Adversaries flood targeted email addresses with an overwhelming volume of messages to disrupt business operations and bury legitimate communications.
